title: Memory walkthrough: pointers and reference aliases
intro: Step through the same statements used in the runnable walkthrough below. Arrows mean “stores the address of.” A reference is shown as another name on the object it aliases—not as a separately reseatable pointer.

steps.note: x and y are two separate int objects with automatic storage duration.
ptr is a pointer object. Its value is the address of x. & takes an address; *ptr would access the int at that address.
Copying the pointer copies its address value, not the int. Both pointers now refer to x.
num is another name for x. The language does not require a separate storage cell for this reference.
Dereferencing ptr selects x. x becomes 100, and num observes that same object.
Reseating ptr changes only ptr. p2 and the reference num still refer to x.
This copies 10 into x. It does not rebind num to y. Equal values do not mean two objects share storage.
p2 still points to x, so x becomes 42. y remains 10.
ptr now has no target. x and y still exist. Never dereference a null pointer.

title: Memory walkthrough: allocation, aliases, and deletion
intro: The pointer variables and dynamically allocated objects have separate lifetimes. “Heap” is the usual implementation term for dynamic storage; locations A and B are symbolic, not real addresses.

steps.note: Two pointer objects exist locally, but neither points to an allocation.
new creates and initializes a dynamic int, then returns its address to p.
Both pointers store the same address. There is still only one dynamically allocated int.
The shared allocation changes to 12. Reading *p would also produce 12.
The int’s lifetime ends and its storage is released. p and alias still exist but are dangling; neither may be used to access the deleted int. The old value is deliberately no longer shown.
Resetting p changes only p. alias is still dangling. Do not dereference it.
Both pointer objects are now null. Resetting pointers is separate from releasing an allocation.
new[] creates a contiguous array of three int elements. values points to its first element.
Index 1 is the second element. values[i] and *(values+i) refer to the same element within bounds.
delete[] releases the whole array. values still exists but is dangling. Match new[] with delete[], not delete.
Both allocations have been released, and all three pointer variables have been reset. No pointer is dereferenced after deletion.
